speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, July 8, consideration in committee of Bill No. 56, to make provision with respect to insurance of

War Risk Insurance
property against war risks and the payment of compensation for war damage-Mr. Usley -Mr. Vien in the chair.
On section 2-Definitions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
When we adjourned last evening I had raised the question of the reason for the deletion of subsection (m) as it stood in the bill sent to the committee. I pointed out that in my judgment the deletion of that paragraph left the bill deficient in an important respect. I also said that I believe the bill as it at present stands is confused, because of the fact that those who drafted the bill were endeavouring to defer to two principles. I desired that before I should consent to the passage of section 2 some explanation should be given which would clarify matters which to me seemed confused.
I think it can be safely laid down as a fundamental principle that no Canadian family should be obliged to suffer inequality of sacrifice for war damage. I believe this bill was designed to take care of that situation so far as it may be possible so to do. There are those who say that equality of sacrifice is completely impossible. Suppose we grant that as a government and as a -parliament we ought to be guided by the general principle that wherever possible we shall ensure equality of sacrifice. This we certainly can do in financial matters.
I think we can lay it down as fundamental with respect to this bill that every Canadian family should be guaranteed the right to continue to possess and to live in its home. That is the first fundamental consideration. The second is that every Canadian community should be guaranteed the right to be able to supply as many people after war damage as it was able to supply before the war damage was done. I gather from the discussions which I heard in the banking and commerce committee and in this house and which I have had with other people that those two principles were in the minds of the men who drafted this bill.
As I understand it, the purpose of the bill is to empower the minister to bring about or to establish or to embody in his policy those two fundamental principles: first that every family in Canada shall be guaranteed the right to continue to live in its home as such; second, that every community in Canada shall be guaranteed the right to be able to support or supply with needed services as many people after war damage as it was able to supply before war damage. If such is the case, the primary object of this bill is to ensure human values rather than financial values. In this respect it differs materially from an ordinary
fire insurance measure. A fire insurance measure aims primarily to reimburse, to the extent of his financial loss, anyone who has suffered damage from fire, the financial loss to-be judged by the value on the open market of the property destroyed. The second objective of a fire insurance measure, I take it, is to enable a fire insurance company to carry the risk, as well as other risks, and not lose money but rather to make money.
If these are the objects of a fire insurance measure, while the object of this measure is fundamentally human values rather than financial values, it becomes apparent that if the principles which govern the drafting of a fire insurance measure are applied to this measure there will be inconsistency and confusion. I believe that in at least two respects the principles governing the drafting of fire insurance measures are being applied in this bill as a means of governing the kind of measure which this shall be.
I maintain that we need to define clearly what we mean by values. How important this is may be seen by reference to section 7, subsection 1, where the whole meaning and intent and efficacy of the measure depends entirely on the definition of "diminution of value" in the third line. If there is no means of determining what that value is, how can the clause have any meaning? How can the bill have any meaning? It may be contended that this bill is aimed to pay its way just as a fire insurance measure aims to pay its way. This measure by section 7 empowers the minister, for example, to pay $3,000 to one who has sustained war damage. No reference is made to the necessity of the individual who sustained the damage having taken out an insurance policy; the minister is empowered, without any reservation, to pay $3,000 in consideration of war damage. This seems to indicate quite clearly that we are not concerned about making the whole scheme pay. If we are not aiming to make the whole scheme pay, then we do not need to be greatly concerned with the definition of value as it stood in the original bill. The original bill defined "value" as the value which the property would bring in the open market. I maintain that for the purpose of this measure that is not a meaning of value that we are at all concerned about.
Again we find in section 10 an exception of $50; that is, if the extent of the damage is less than $50 no payment is to be made. I maintain that that exception might be quite in order in a fire insurance measure, a regular policy of a fire insurance company, but it is inconsistent with the spirit and purpose of this bill.

War Risk Insurance

May I turn for a moment to a discussion of the question of value as I think it should be. There are two main types of value with respect to properties such as dwellings. There is the social or prestige value, and there is the utility or service value. We might add another class of value, namely, the combination of the two. To illustrate what is in my mind, I would refer to a case which came under my observation. A young couple purchased a house for $450 when they were first married. They lived in it for fifteen years. As several children had come along they had found it impossible to buy a more commodious home. At the end of fifteen years they simply had to have more room. They raised up the house and put under it a basement with a seven-foot clearance, large enough to make possible a considerable addition to the house. As the house then stood it had cost them about $850. They had to let the house stand as it was, without improvements for several years. By that time the resale value on the open market would be hardly more than $150, the amount for which a person could sell the material if he salvaged the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: There is far too much conversation going on in the chamber.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am surely glad you pointed that out, because the hon. gentlemen who are. talking have almost completely destroyed my ability to present this matter this afternoon. If they wrant to talk, I think they should go outside. I could hardly hear what you were saying, Mr. Chairman.
As I was pointing out, the house I have in mind cost the family $850, plus their work, but if they had had to sell it on the open market they would have been able to obtain only $150 or $200 for it. If this house were destroyed because of the war, it is conceivable that all that family would get as full compensation would be $150 or $200. This would mean that they would have insufficient money to build a new house. They would have to suffer an almost complete loss; in effect, they would be on the street. This house as it stood, while it might be impossible to sell it for anything near what it was worth, had a value to that family of a house which might have cost $2,500 because in it they were able to shelter their children and get by, as many Canadian families have to get by. If this house, which cost $850 and had a service or utility value to them of $2,500, were damaged to the extent of $49. according to this bill these people would
[Mr. Blackmore.)
receive nothing for damage which might render their place of residence entirely uninhabitable.
I think the illustration I have given is sufficient to show that as the bill now stands it is a rich man's bill, not a poor man's bill; that the application of the bill would bring into existence many inequalities and injustices. In order to show how many glaring inequalities might spring out of the application of the bill, may I point out that section 7 permits the minister to pay $3,000 for damages. As long as that section remains as it is, and I have no objection to it, a man with a house costing $3,000 which was destroyed would receive the full $3,000. In other words, he would have 100 per cent protection under this bill. There are many well-to-do Canadians who would come in his class. They would own houses costing from $3,000 to $5,000.
There are other Canadians who are a little better off and who own houses costing from $6,000 to $10,000. If these houses are damaged in the war the owners will receive compensation which will go a long way toward covering the cost of repairing the damage. They will receive substantial benefits under the bill. It must be borne in mind that the man with the $3,000 house is probably in receipt of a salary of $3,000 a year, and consequently would be in a better position to repair damage than a man in the lower income brackets. The man who owns a house costing $6,000 or $7,000 is probably getting in the neighbourhood of $6,000 or $7,000 a year, and therefore would be able to repair any damage done to his house. When these facts are considered it becomes more evident how unjust this bill will be to a person owning a house worth only $450 which sustains damage of, we will say, $49. Such a man probably is receiving only a very small income and is not in position to rebuild or repair his house. His family is probably such that he has had to struggle all the time in order to make ends meet. This man will receive perhaps no recompense at all if the damage is under $50. If the damage amounts to $100 and he receives reimbursement he will not be much better off. He certainly would not be relatively as well off as the man with the house costing $3,000, or the still more fortunate man with the house costing $6,000 or $8,000, and which sustained damage to the extent of $3,000.
As the bill stands at the present time I think it is quite unjust. It discriminates against the poor man in favour of the rich man. I believe it should be amended in two important respects. It should be stipulated definitely in the bill just what is meant by

War Risk Insurance
value; I suggest that the wording of this stipulation should take some such form as this:
That the value with reference to a property means the amount which would be required to restore the property to the degree of capacity for utility or serviceability or habitability which the property had before it was damaged.
In such case if the house to which I refer, which cost $850 to construct and which enabled a considerable family to get by, were damaged, we will say to the extent of only $100, the bill would permit the minister to restore the house to a condition in which it would be able to render the same service to the family occupying it that it had rendered before the damage was sustained, regardless of the amount it might sell for on the open market. If that definition of value, or a similar one, were embodied in the bill, I believe it would help greatly.
Then I think the bill should be modified to eliminate almost entirely the $50 exemption. Many a poor man is living in a house that would scarcely sell for $200 on the open market. I think it is grossly unfair to refuse to pay any damages which are under $50 in value. Suppose the chimney were destroyed, or the door on the porch blown off, or a hole made in the basement; if the total damage were assessed at less than $50, that man would get nothing, and it might be impossible for him and his family to rebuild the dwelling so as to make it habitable.
Hon. members may imagine that there are not many Canadian people who live in houses of as small a value as I have indicated. But all they need to do is to go through the woods to see the number of very inexpensive shacks in which people are living, or see in the wide areas of the west the inexpensive shacks in which farmers and landowners are endeavouring to get by, or go through the outskirts of many of our small towns to realize the number of small, inadequate habitations in which many Canadian people are struggling to live. Even in this great city of Ottawa and our next door neighbour you will find a surprisingly large percentage of houses that are very cheap and probably assessed at anywhere from $175 to $250. If a dwelling of that sort were damaged to the extent of 10 per cent of its value, from a money standpoint that might seem very small, but from the standpoint of human values, from the standpoint of the ability of the family to continue to live in the house after the damage was done, or to rebuild it so that it would be in as good a condition as it was before it was bombed, it will easily be seen that it would be grossly unfair to apply rigidly this limitation that nothing shall be paid unless the damage is over $50.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that the modifications which I feel should be made in the bill can be brought up under other sections. With that understanding I would say to the minister that I am prepared to allow section 2 to pass, and I will bring up the matters I have in mind under subsequent sections where perhaps they can be more appropriately dealt with.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise not to discuss the questions raised by the hon. member for Lethbridge, but to point out that this is the ninth day of July and we are in the sixth month of the session. This is a business proposition we are discussing ; it is not in any sense a political question. While members have quite properly occupied a substantial amount of time in discussing the rights of fishermen to protection, I do think the time has arrived when we as business men ought to get down to putting this bill through on its merits so that we can bring this session to a conclusion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
I should like to rise in support of what the hon. member for Lethbridge has said in respect to the valuation of houses and the damage that may be done in the case of a wealthy man's home as compared with the home of a poor man.
I see no reason why we should not indemnify everyone in Canada, be he fisherman, tradesman, farmer or what have you, for every cent of loss that may be caused through war damage, bombing, and so forth. I know that we have spent a good deal of time on this bill, but I am perfectly satisfied that we do not 3ret realize the serious damage that may be caused, since we are so far distant from actual bombing. But sometimes the seriousness of it can be brought home to us very forcibly. The other day I received a letter from my mother in England, telling me that my mother and father had been bombed out. They escaped or were rescued from the debris with nothing but the clothes on their backs. I am going to suggest to you, sir, that if the cities of Canada were afflicted with the bombings that have taken place in other parts of the world every member of parliament would be in his seat urging the government to pay compensation for any type of war damage sustained by our people. That letter from my mother brought the seriousness of the situation home very forcibly to me.
I assume that should there be much bombing of Canadian cities there would be set up an administration which would be running all over the place trying to adjust claims and to decide whether a window is worth 75 cents or $5, and all that sort of thing. We have had that sort of machinery
War Risk Insurance

set up in connection with the bonuses for agriculture in Canada, some of which are not yet paid. The people of this country would not stand for anything like that if this country were going through a bombing. I refer again to my mother's letter. In spite of the fact that my mother and father had nothing left in the world, they said, "The government administration here in England in behalf of bombed-out victims is marvellous." I sent my mother and father a little money, not because they were bombed out, but because I thought they needed it. It arrived a few days after they had lost everything, and my mother said, "You do not need to send us any more money, because we are well provided for." I know that there is a bombed^ out victims' fund, but my mother went on to say, "The government are very apt to visit us and discover just what our loss may be, and urge us to put in our claim now." That bit of news gladdened my heart, and I trust that after this bill is passed the government will see to it that those who are the victims of war damage will not have to worry, worry, worry, as to when their claims will be settled and how much they are to get.
During the discussion on this bill I have noticed, as no doubt other hon. members have, that there seems to be a fear on the part of the government as to whether they will be able to meet all these claims. You see, Mr. Chairman, it is the same old story: Can we afford to pay for the damage done? It is the same old story-we have no money. It does not make any difference how much lumber or stone or cement we have for repairs, or how much skilled labour is available; we are afraid that maybe we will not have the money. The same financial advisers who were advising the government in pre-war depression years are advising them to-day, and are doing so in respect to the financing involved in the present bill, which may be described as partly a postwar measure.
I stand with the hon. member for Lethbridge in what he has asked the committee to do.
I go further, and say that every nickel of damage done to anyone in Canada, be he fisherman, farmer or anyone else, should be paid promptly; and let our people know that if war should come to our shores we have a government which will stop at nothing to give them adequate and complete compensation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Macleod has just told us about his parents who were bombed out in England. I will take a couple of minutes to speak of a section of our Canadian people who have been blasted and bombed ever since Canada became Canada, and I see that they are being bombed once 
more on this occasion. I am referring now to paragraph (j) (ii). If this legislation goes through as it is at the present time, "growing crops, plants and trees" will be excluded from the benefits of the measure. I think the committee is well aware of the fact that 90 per cent of farmers are in debt up to their necks, in some cases a little deeper. One of my neighbours in Paradise Valley, who came to this country fairly recently, gave me a plan which he thought could be put into operation to burn out the crops of the countries which have been overrun by Germany. If that plan is feasible over there, as I believe to a certain extent it is, then it is possible that our enemies may put it into effect and burn out our crops here. A man with a $450 house who has $45 damage done to it has sustained a loss of 10 per cent of the value of his property; the man with a $4,500 house who sustains a loss of $450 has sustained only a 10 per cent loss. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
What is

. . . specifying the time at which any payment under this act or under any contract of insurance shall be made. . . .
And then the overriding part which provides:	.
. . . the minister may, in his discretion, pay the whole or any part of any moneys payable under this act or under any contract of insurance at a time earlier than the time specified in such regulation.
Has the minister in mind the usual standard regulations contained in insurance policies, which I think would be reasonably satisfactory? If he has any other provision in view, I think we ought to know what they are.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
What was contemplated
under this scheme of insurance was to defer the restoration of property until after the war. In England they found that it was perhaps inadvisable to rebuild at once; they might be bombed again, and there were other reasons for deferring as much construction as possible. I think this is the section which provides for the making of the regulations for deferring payment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: It does not just say, "for deferring payment"; it says, "specifying the time." Is it the minister's idea that it might become, in the case of a tremendous bombardment, too onerous and perhaps unwise, having regard to the danger of threatened rebombardment, to replace and rebuild?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: And he only limits that, in the concluding portion of the paragraph, to an exercise of discretion in himself, or to avoid undue hardship, or if the amount does not exceed the sum of $400. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: It is an alternative.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: Oh, yes, it is an alternative, but in any event I would assume that the minister would exercise a discretion in the case of the amount payable not exceeding $400. That, of course, is a small loss. Why should $400 be the limit? I think the amount should be a little more liberal in the case of rebuilding or repairing small houses where the damage would be more than $400.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: Yes; well, the minister has the right to do that for the purpose of avoiding undue hardship. He may pay at once, if the sum is under $400, whether there would be any hardship or not from withholding payment. But in all cases of undue hardship the minister has a discretion to bring the time of payment back before the period provided for in the regulations. I think the general idea of the section is that the normal thing will be to make regulations deferring the time for payment of loss, with the proviso that nevertheless the loss may be paid at once to avoid undue hardship; or, whether undue hardship exists or not, it may be paid at once if the amount involved is under $400. There would not be any sense in withholding these small sums.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
Has the government any definite policy with regard to administering this section? It does seem, from what the minister has said, that the tendency will be to withhold payments until after the war. The war may last a long time, and in the meantime people in British Columbia and Nova Scotia who lose their houses will need shelter and furniture and chattels of various kinds. I suggest to the minister that the policy of the government may not be wise in regard to this section, that there should not be so much emphasis placed on withholding payment until after the war. That may apply very well in Great Britain, and I assume that this policy is simply copying the policy of Great Britain.

War Risk Insurance
I doubt very much, however, whether it is wise here in Canada. I sugggest that the minister be not too quick in adopting the policy of holding back until after the war; it may turn out to be very unwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: We cannot tell what the policy will be until we see what happens. This is the policy followed in England, and it is a good thing to defer building and so on as much as possible until after the war, because the more building you do now, the more drain you make on materials and labour and so forth. On the other hand, of course that cannot be carried to the point where people are left drifting around without any shelter. All these factors will be taken into consideration. The English policy is embodied in this section; and if the legislation comes into play at all, if there is bombardment doing damage here, I do not see any reason why the English policy is not the right policy for this country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
What is the meaning of the words, "if he is satisfied either that the replacement or repair of the property damaged is expedient in the public interest?" It is not in the public interest that we should have this bill at all. It is not expedient; this is the wrong time for it. It will be observed that the minister has power to make rules and regulations. The details are set out at the foot of page 11 of the bill, section 33, which must be read into subsection 1 of section 11. I would point out that the insurance companies are protected while the government is not. The companies are backed by indirect guarantee of the government. Suppose the owner of certain property becomes a soldier. What happens then, if default is made? The minister said yesterday that he could have done all this by order in council under the War Measures Act. If so, what is the use of us? He threatened us with the War Measures Act, if you please, if we continued to insist on safeguards. If you ask any questions under this bill you are threatened with something of the sort.
A large body of public opinion is wondering how the government can afford money for such an undertaking as this in conjunction with the insurance companies. Is it expedient and in the public interest that this parliament should put into the hands of the governor in council the power to spend up to $400 on such a risk or contract or policy for such a purpose? I say it is not, and this is not the time. According to the minister's report that is what can happen. I protest against this way of doing business. I protest against the creation of more boards of control and a whole lot of officials, in this instance enabling
44561-257J
the government to pay out as much as $400 for such a purpose and in such a way. That is a lot of money. In my opinion this section, indeed the whole bill, should be rejected. It is not one that this committee should sanction at the present time. You, Mr. Chairman, are a lawyer, and you know, as all lawyers know, the difficulties that arise in connection with contracts' of insurance on property and with insurance companies. On the back of the contract the insurance company sets out a long list of rules and restrictions to be read into the policy and contract, and I predict that the average working man who seeks to take advantage of this legislation will not know the meaning of it. He will not know what it is all about if he comes under this insurance scheme and has a policy. In my opinion the whole scheme is launched for the benefit of the insurance companies, and at greater cost to give them the cream of the business. It seems to me that the officials in the minister's department are simply creating further burdens to be put on the shoulders of the Canadian tapayer, at a time when it is neither expedient nor in the best interest of the public that we should pass a law of this kind. I do not believe in this bill; I do not believe it will fulfil the purpose for which it is proposed; I do not believe it is in the interests of the working classes of the country. In my opinion they will not be protected under this measure. On any contract of insurance with companies that are under contract with the government to do this work and take these risks, are the companies solvent, and can they carry out their undertakings.

In view of the discussion that took place just before we rose at six o'clock I should like to move that the amendment I then proposed be amended by changing the words "great lakes" to "inland waters," so that the amendment would read "between two Canadian ports on inland waters shall at all times during the transit."
Mr. O'NEILL: Would that exclude shipments going to Vancouver island, or from Vancouver to Nanaimo, or between Vancouver and Victoria?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: In those cases neither the goods nor the ships are insurable. Let me make that clear. The bill does not provide insurance for ships at all anywhere, but there is a situation with regard to goods on inland waters which I thought made it very desirable to provide that goods on inland waters should be subject to the provisions of this bill. That is so for various reasons. In the first place there is the reason of convenience. One of the most important commodities concerned is grain. It is covered while in the elevators, and sometimes it is stored in boats on the great lakes. It would be very inconvenient-and there did not seem to be very much reason for doing so-to take off this insurance when the grain left the elevator and put it on again when the grain was put on shore somewhere else. So I thought we should cover the goods in transit in Canada. Goods on railways in Canada, which railways are competing with the boats, are insurable under this bill; and I thought it desirable, even though we have taken ships out of the bill entirely as I felt we had to do, to leave the insurance on goods which are in transit in Canada. This simply says that a movement of goods across the boundary line and back again between two points in inland waters, which would be between two points on the great lakes or between a point on the great lakes and a point on a river, shall still be deemed to be a movement within Canada. In the same way a movement on the Canadian Pacific railway or the Canadian National railway which starts in Canada and ends in Canada, shall be deemed to be a movement in Canada even though it crosses United States territory. That is all this amendment does.

I would invite the Minister of Justice to give us the benefit of his opinion. I have great respect for the minister's position in the profession. I am sure any contribution he would make to this discussion would be of great value.

I know, however, that difficulties have been experienced to a certain degree in connection with false claims made against the workmen's compensation boards, which have had to prosecute persons for attempting to obtain money by false pretences, and it is a cumbersome procedure to have to resort to in a good many of these cases. If there had been such a provision as this, guarding against claims made falsely, I know it would have been a great convenience. The offence of obtaining or attempting to obtain money by false pretences has to be proceeded on under the code by way of indictment; that method is cumbersome, and a speedy method of dealing with small claims improperly asserted would seem to be more convenient. This provision would not oust the other, whenever there were grounds that would seem to warrant the more solemn form of indictment under the criminal code.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

LAURENT: Not exactly on the ground of expediency, but on the ground of this being a more convenient method of dealing with an attempt at an offence that may not involve a large amount but that still should be prosecuted. speechtext: Could the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Justice tell us if there is any other act on the statute books that goes as far as this is going? This seems to be something new. There is nothing that I know of in the general insurance law, particularly of Ontario, which is now the common law of all provinces, that is comparable to this section. As I remember the general law, the common law

War Risk Insurance
applies. That is to say, if there is something obtained by fraud and it can be shown that it is fraudulent, that which has been obtained wrongfully is withdrawn. But this section goes further than that. I doubt if it is possible to make one of the usual claims under an insurance policy and at the conclusion of it be prepared to guarantee that every statement is correct. I imagine that a large percentage of such claims would show that something said therein was inaccurate and that the person who made the claim knew it. This is so because of the difficulty of making a claim. This bill does not change the procedure; this changes the substantive law, and it provides a penalty equal for a white lie or a black lie, equal for a big lie or a small lie; anything which is knowingly done, no matter how small it may be. The penalty is the loss of the entire claim, not that portion of the claim which was supported by fraud or that portion which was collected as the result of fraud; the untruth and the knowing untruth of any statement disentitles the insured to all the benefits. I think that is extreme, unnecessary and inadvisable. I believe we should rely on the common law.

This section goes farther and makes liable also the person who helps out the person who is getting the money, the third party. This may be a witness, an agent or an accomplice. That probably is the chief merit of the section; it is probably in that clause that lies the chief necessity for the section. But apart from that altogether, it is desirable, and it certainly does no harm to create a statutory offence which is punishable upon summary conviction instead of putting the crown to the necessity of laying an information, seeking a commitment and going before a jury, with all the expense and delay that that entails.

I should think that if a fraudulent statement is made, it would be a black lie, and it is only black lies that are covered by the section. A claim may be made for insurance on a house by the head of the household. He may give false evidence and, if there is a family, the loss will fall not only upon that individual, but upon the family as well. speechtext: The Department of Justice knows when a case is patently frivolous, and it would be the proper thing to refuse a fiat. But I would not counsel disturbance of the practice of requiring a fiat. If we overthrow that principle we are going to do a lot of overthrowing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
I agree with that, but the whole thing goes back to the day when you could not sue the crown. The crown's person and property and everything else were sacrosanct. It was a matter

not of right but of grace to be able to get compensation from the crown. I suggest, however, that we have gone a long way from that, and we can go still further without doing great violence to the principle involved. We can go a long way in doing justice to the subject as against the crown. The minister has correctly stated that an excellent practice has been established over a period of years by the crown in the right of the dominion in the granting of fiats. I have brought a few actions against the crown, and I have never been refused a fiat. I will tell the committee what I have encountered. I have encountered a good deal of delay. That I do not attribute to the crown itself; I attribute it to what I may call, for lack of a better term, the system of red tape that obtains in government departments. But the situation is quite different with respect to provincial governments. There, a denial of justice often occurs. In my view, the day is coming in this country when the subject will have the right to sue the crown without the necessity of obtaining a fiat; without praying that right be done, and without the easement of fiat justitia. That day, I think, should be here very soon.
The minister says that the insurer has a contractual relation with the crown, and I would agree; that would be the basis upon which the claim would be made. I believe a just claim ought to be facilitated. If the minister takes exception to putting that provision in this special bill, perhaps he is right; but the day is coming when it will not be necessary to pray that justice be done in this country as against the crown. I have often thought, too, that claims against the crown ought not to be limited to the crown's own court, the exchequer court. The day is coming in this country when we ought to be able to sue the crown in the provincial courts of the country, for there is just as much justice done there as in the exchequer court. I say that with no intention of reflecting on the exchequer court, which I have found to be a very fine court in which to practise. But I am inclined to say to my hon. friend the member for Lake Centre that perhaps he could not just put that provision in this statute at this time without overhauling the whole machineiy in regard to claims against the crown. I do say that the position should be reviewed, especially now that the crown has gone into big business-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY

I am not sure that these remarks will be pleasing to the hon. member for Lake Centre, but I do not think you could make a special exception with regard to this statute.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
With deference, I do not agree with the view of the leader of the opposition, nor is his view that of the Canadian Bar association. The view of the bar association is that the time has come when the subject should, as of right, have the privilege to take action against the crown. In this particular instance we have the crown entering into a contractual relationship with the subject, and placing the subject in the position that he is denied his right of recourse to the courts unless the crown grants him that right.
It has not been the experience of everyone that the crown has allowed the subject to obtain his rights by the granting of a fiat. I know of one very interesting case in connection with the Indians of this country. The Indians of western Canada obtained certain rights under a treaty, at the time when the great west from the Hudson bay to the Rocky mountains was ceded by the Indian tribes to Her Majesty Queen Victoria. In 1937 or 1938 those tribes found themselves in the position that the dominion government was derelict in its duty in not carrying out its obligations under that treaty and the act, and finally, after a very lengthy debate, the Indians of Mistawasis reserve were granted a fiat. The trial took place, and the judgment handed down was in favour of the tribe, to the extent of some $18,000. Then Indian tribes on another reserve in Saskatchewan, being in the identical position of the Indian tribe at Mistawasis, asked the crown for the right to take proceedings to recover the moneys due them, and for the assertion of their rights. To-day those Indians are in the position of still being denied justice, because of the fact that the crown has taken advantage of its rights and has denied them a fiat, or, in other words, has denied them recourse to the courts.
In recent years there has been a definite trend away from the courts, and I think the time has come when we in parliament should grant every individual the right of recourse to the courts of this land, and should not place any individual in a position where his rights may be determined by some administrative body or by a minister of the crown.
I think the time has come when the whole matter should be canvassed, the whole situation looked into, in order to assure to the subject the right he is being denied in ever-increasing measure-that is, an appeal to the courts as a consequence of administrative bodies being set up. The other day the Minister of Finance referred to the fact that parliament does not occupy the position now that it occupied once. I think one reason for that situation is that we as members of parliament are too prone to allow matters with which we should deal to be placed in the hands of administrative bodies, independent of parliament and responsible not to parliament but, indirectly, to the minister. In this case what we are actually doing is allowing the minister to set up an advisory council responsible only to himself, and to no one else, to determine the rights of individuals. Against that I protest.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
I am afraid that the advisory committee which is being appointed under this celebrated excursion into state socialism will mean nothing but a lot of figureheads run by bureaucrat officials, with the power centred in the minister and the governor general in council. We know what happens in actual practice. Under the Insurance Act the superintendent of insurance has jurisdiction over all these various insurance companies-fire insurance companies, life insurance companies and all the rest of them. We know that every insurance company, every bank, every trust company, every loan company or every other company of this kind has an advisory committee. No insurance company should be enabled to qualify for a certificate by reason of the money it may make out of the administration of this particular measure.
The Home bank, which was allied with an insurance and trust company, had an advisory committee, and all the inspection of it was of no effect whatever. Before the bank failed I was told that every bank or insurance company had an advisory committee and drastic federal inspection, and I can tell you that it will be hard to get good men on the advisory committee to be appointed under this bill, and they will be nothing but a lot of figureheads. You have to see the set-up of the whole statute to see how an advisory committee fits into the general set-up and structure of the bill. Under the set-up the governor in council, that is the minister, has the power to make rules and regulations and is in drastic control. On page 11 of the bill you see regulations that will be read into the section regarding the appointment of the advisory
War Risk Insurance

committee to advise the minister in the administration. But who is going to select this committee to supervise him and the legislation? The minister himself will have all control. I have seen some of these advisory committees, they and their set-up and the functions given them let this parliament and the banks and the loan and insurance and trust companies in for considerable criticism the way they are all interlocked.
I have been in parliament for a long time. I have seen something of the way in which this committee and parliament go over these measures. They read very well technically and in theory; the language is legal, but in practice they do not work out and we are not secure. The advisory committees of some of these banks and insurance companies and all that kind of thing who will bid for this work and contract from the minister are interlocked; trusts and combines have been flourishing like a green bay tree here in Canada ever since I came to this parliament. Instead of leaving these advisory committees to go over the contracts with the insurance company and pick out the company that in the opinion of the advisory committee is the best company to give security to the government and the policyholders who pay premiums, we are going to leave it with the minister or the governor in council; it will be a political appointment to administer a political measure. That feature of inspection and regulation was criticized by Sir Robert Borden in connection with the decennial revision of the Bank Act. These committees of an advisory nature are set up under the Bank Act and various other statutes. Are you going to leave it to these advisory committees to lay down the terms and conditions of administration of the bill? The minister is here to-day and away to-morrow. We have had two ministers of finance in less than two years. His department with him as the fountainhead, will administer this measure. He has departmental officials to advise him, because he cannot do the work himself, and when it comes to the question, "What shall we refer to this advisory committee?" as far as administration goes you will find there will be very little to refer to them. All they will have to do will be to agree to what has been done over their heads. I am very doubtful about the solvency of this fund from the start and whether you will be able to get able men to act on such an advisory committee under such a political set-up, where their hands are tied behind their backs and they have no real active authority. We have set up insurance companies under private ownership, and now the government is, by this legislation, embarking upon the field of public

ownership. You have first a very wise act, the Unemployment Insurance Act, which no doubt will be a blessing in the years to come, but in this case the government should be very careful in this new excursion into state socialism. In letting this class of insurance in war time out to private companies to administer, we are on doubtful ground, and it will lead to a lot of litigation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
I think I should not let this occasion go by without adding my commendation of the viewpoint of the hon. member for Lake Centre concerning the fiat. I think this case is different from many cases where fiats are required as petitions of right against the crown. When you analyse the bill you realize that the insurance companies with their adjusters are handling a particular portion of the administration of this bill, determining to a very great extent the rights of individuals who claim to have suffered by virtue of war activities. Let us assume that in a certain municipality or locality the adjuster, looking into the facts and circumstances, does not give the assured the decision that he feels he should have. The assured has to apply through his counsel to the crown, really to the Minister of Justice, for permission to sue the crown. As the hon. member for Lake Centre has said, the government has been delegating to boards, arbitrators and commissions a great many functions that should be administered by members of the House of Commons, by the people through their own spokesmen. Here we have a survival of the old autocratic role of former kings, the old way long since superseded in almost every other department of law, whereby you cannot sue the king-"The king can do no wrong". We have this relic remaining in a measure under which the government is actually going into the contracting business.
The fiat or petition of right procedure, the order, "let justice be done" as against the crown, the Minister of Finance says should be or is being continued. If this parliament is afraid to break that tradition, we are not keeping in tune with present-day views concerning the welfare of the people of Canada. When the crown places the responsibility of administering the measure on an insurance company under its officers or trained men, whether they be adjusters, administrators or advisory committee, it is going a long way from the tradition or the position taken by parliament when the petition of right or fiat was instituted. It stretches beyond all possibility of comprehension of a parliament of that day. That being the case, and when the government is entering into contracts

War Risk Insurance
such as we are dealing with, in view of the delay and the extra expense caused to the insured through such matters being tried by the exchequer court-and I have no complaint against that-surely the time has come that the courts of the provinces, the ordinary civil courts, with the respect in which they are held, can adjudicate upon such problems. Even under war-time conditions this brings a very fit and proper opportunity for hon. members to give to the people of Canada the assurance that this house has confidence in our provincial courts, and the people should have the right to seek their remedy as against the crown and the insurance companies in the same court as they do against their neighbour. Therefore I should very much like to add my commendation and exhortation to that of the hon. member for Lake Centre in asking that this matter of the petition of right and fiat be reconsidered by the government. Let us break away from this procedure now, and let right be done through the ordinary courts of the land.

The minister may refer to the advisory committee any application to enter into a contract of insurance under which the maximum amount of indemnity which may be payable exceeds two hundred and fifty thousand dollars. . . .
I also see that the minister "may" refer to the advisory committee all matters relative to the rate of premiums to be charged. I think the word should be "shall". In the ordinary insurance company there would be a board of directors which would adjudicate on such matters as that. Here you have one supervisor of insurance, and I think it ought to be obligatory upon him or the minister to refer matters such as this to the advisory committee.

but such deduction shall only be allowed to the extent that the total taxes payable by the insured under the said act are thereby diminished by 40 per centum of the said premium.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: I want hon. members of this committee to understand the position we shall be in if these words are not restored. In the budget provision there is an excess profits tax of 100 per cent, with 20 per cent returnable. These changes in the excess profits tax throw a very large proportion of the corporations doing business in Canada into such a class that any premium that might be paid for war risk insurance will be paid out of excess profits which are taxable 100 per cent. In other words, if this clause remains as it is in the bill, without the restoration of these words, the crown will be giving free coverage but for the 20 per cent returnable.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: Apparently we are going to have a debate on this. So far as I am concerned, I cannot possibly agree to having the clause remain as it is.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: There is a rule of reason about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Do not let us do something that will be ridiculous. Let us forget the 20 per cent returnable feature for a moment and consider just the 100 per cent excess profits tax. Mr. Matson goes to a company and says, "we would like you to put on some war risk insurance". The company may see fit to put on $1,000,000 worth of war risk insurance. If the premium is, say 25 cents per $100, it would amount to $2,500. If the company did not pay that $2,500 to Mr. Matson as premium, they would pay the full $2,500 to Mr. Fraser Elliott as excess profits tax. If they paid it to Mr. Fraser Elliott as excess profits tax, the crown would not be

liable to make good their SI,000,000; if they paid it to Mr. Matson, the crown would be liable. In other words, if you leave out the 20 per cent returnable feature, they are getting free coverage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
The same is true of ordinary fire insurance premiums.
Mr. ILSLEY; But the fire insurance premiums are not being paid to the crown. We cannot help that under the rules. I certainly am not going to be a party to giving free coverage, apart from the 20 per cent returnable provision, which does effect a slight modification. With this section as it is we are setting up a scheme whereby we would give free coverage to, I would say, nine-tenths of the corporations in Canada. That would be the situation under the new excess profits tax. Under the old tax it might have been only one-quarter or one-tenth, I do not know, but there were very few corporations of which it could be said that the premiums would be paid out of excess profits. Now it would apply to most of them. I want all corporations to be treated the same. It must be borne in mind that if I am right in my figure and there are nine-tenths of the companies in that category, there would be one-tenth not in that category. That one-tenth would pay Mr. Matson a premium and would reduce their tax liability by only 40 per cent of that premium because their rate is 40 per cent. I am submitting that the rate for all companies should be such that the tax saving because of paying a premium would be 40 per cent of the premium instead of having it 40 per cent for only a small class of companies and 100 per cent for nearly all classes. I think anything else would be utterly indefensible, and I do not see how we could defend it to the people. I am going to move that the words be restored.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: The minister admits that ordinary insurance costs would be deductible under any taxation law, and I think it would be shocking if they were not.

speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: Any reasonable operating cost for fire insurance purposes ought to be a deduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: They do not allow war risk premiums in England.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
I do not care what they do in England. We are talking about Canada. In England they need the money. We need the money here, and that is the basis of the minister's whole claim. It is simply the doctrine of ex necessitate. It is not a question of justice at all. If you will examine and analyse the doctrine put forward by the minister, you will find that it simply is a case of saying, "I raise the taxes of this country. I want this money." That is the basis of his whole scheme. I admit we need the money; and if it is just and equitable that we should have it by this, method, well, then, let us have it. But the same thing might be argued in respect of other expenses. Take the depreciation allowance on machinery. There is no reason why, if we need the money, we should not cut down the allowances made for depreciation. I remember that during the depression certain public utilities, like telephone companies, were operating under standard depreciation systems. A telephone company is subject to storms and other untoward circumstances which may cause a loss of thousand of dollars in two or three hours. The company has to sustain that loss, and therefore it is allowed a high rate of depreciation to cover these unforeseen circumstances. But on the doctrine of necessity we should cut down the allowance that is made. If the minister bases himself on the principle that we have to have this money, no matter where the chips fall, I have little more to say.
But let me ask the minister this. This government has established a cost-of-living bonus system for wages, and we are about to have a new application of that system. I have no objection to that because, willy-nilly, the cost of living is rising and will continue to rise in this country, let the government resort to whatever expedients it will, for example, subsidies that are going to cost this country perhaps $150 million or more. The minister allows this bonus for wages to be deducted 100 per cent for excess profit tax purposes. Therefore it might be argued with

War Risk Insurance
just as much force and effect that the treasury is bearing the cost of these bonuses. Let us have a fair application of the principle.
Here is an expense brought upon a property owner by no cause of his own. The country is at war; he undertakes to protect himself or his shareholders by war risk insurance, and that costs money. That, I say, on principle is just as much an expense as the salary of the janitor of the building and certainly just as much a deductible expense as the cost-of-living bonus which this government forces employers to pay. If this deduction is to be put back on the basis as originally drafted, then I suggest that the minister should deal with all in the same way.
What will happen? A man will have to pay this out of his capital. He cannot pay it out of his deductible operating expenses, and how long can that go on if the war lasts for any length of time, and if there is one deduction after another, and another after another, and another after another, payable out of capital? What is going to become, if that goes on, of these companies which give the necessary employment to the people of this country? If it is all going to go in taxation, let the hide go along with the carcase. It does not matter very much to me personally. I am simply speaking in support of a principle -which I think is sound, and evidently that is what the banking committee thought.

speechtext: By a very slim majority.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
It is no use to say that it was a slim majority. It is the democratic principle that the majority rules. The principle of the thing must have appealed to the members of the banking committee. Of course, if the minister is so inflexible that he is bound to have this thing, he can put it through by force, by the majority in this chamber who would no doubt vote this amendment back into the bill again. But in every other case the minister has adopted amendments suggested by the committee.
I do not know by how much the treasury will be affected; I have no idea of what it will run to in dollars and cents. But I do say that the minister in reaffirming the original proposal is violating a principle which has been in the income tax law as long as we have had it-absolutely-and if he is going to do it in this case, he will have to revise his whole outlook. I can think of other cases where he will have to take some steps to protect the treasury for a similar reason. Why should he single out the case of those who are obliged to take
out insurance by circumstances beyond their control, if they want to protect their property and cannot get protection anywhere else, and that will often be the case. Why should he penalize them? Why not make the same rule applicable to any kind of insurance? Employers' liability-I suppose we do not have that now since workmen's compensation acts have come into force in all the provinces -was an operating expense under the Income Tax Act. Ordinary fire insurance is the most apt illustration. If a company is entitled to deduct ordinary fire insurance, it is entitled to deduct war risk insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
I have the English act before me. Section 84 provides:
No sum shall be deducted in computing the amount of the profits or gains of any person for any purpose of the income tax acts or the profits of any person for the purposes of the national defence contribution or for the purposes of excess profits tax, and no sum shall be included in computing . . .
Et cetera, et cetera.
... in respect of-
(i) any payment made in pr towards the discharge of any liability imposed on him under Part 1 of this act-
And so forth. The note to the section reads as follows:
The contributions and premiums payable under this act are treated as capital payments and are accordingly not allowed as an expense for the purposes of income tax, national defence contribution or excess profits tax. This is in contrast to an ordinary fire insurance premium, for instance, which is allowable as an expense for such purposes.
It was represented to me by certain officials in the preparation of this bill that the English rule was the logical rule; that this damage not being of a normal or continuing type, such as fires, but being limited to the period of the war, the risk was of a highly exceptional nature and any payment made should be regarded as a payment made to secure the restoration of capital, and that therefore it should be treated as a capital payment, as was the case in England. On the other hand, other officials felt that it would be too much of a jolt, too much of a shock, to the business community of Canada, to ask them to regard payments for any kind of insurance as capital payments; that once they were told that that was the law they would shy off and we would lose in premiums more than we would gain in taxes, and that on grounds of expediency we should not adopt the English rule. There were others who thought that on grounds of principle we should not adopt the English rule.
After giving the matter some consideration, I felt that there was something to be said for
War Risk Insurance

both points of view, and I thought that a fair arrangement was the one which was suggested in the bill. We would make it deductible; we would allow it to be deducted from incomes for excess profits tax and income tax purposes, but only to such an extent that the tax saving would be 40 per cent. That would be the case with a number of companies-1 think the great majority-at the time the bill was drawn.
But now I have brought in a budget which makes it quite apparent that the great majority of the companies-I said nine-tenths; that is merely a guess, for I have not got my mind down to it-under our new Excess Profits Tax Act, as foreshadowed by the budget, will now be making these payments out of the money which is subject to the 100 per cent rate. In other words, they will simply be withdrawing the money from us and paying it to us and getting a coverage. That is not what we are doing for anybody else. That is not what we are doing for the little man, or for the man not in business. I must make that statement always subject to this, that that is not quite true, by virtue of the fact that 20 per cent will be returnable, but that is such a small factor in the situation. Still, if I use the term 80 per cent instead of 100 per cent tax, we would have a great discrimination between one set of companies which are getting a tax advantage of 80 cents in every dollar they pay us, in effect merely paying us one-fifth of the premium we charge, and the other companies which are getting an advantage of 40 cents in every dollar, in effect paying us three-fifths of the premium we charge them.
The hon. gentleman says it is merely a treasury matter, a matter of trying to grab the money or keep the money. It is not that at all; it is a case of fairness; and if hon. members would divest themselves of their traditional habits of thought about these things and look at the matter freshly, how could they go out and defend it? How could I go out and defend it? If we went to a big company we might insure some property for fifty million dollars instead of a million dollars. Then the premium would be fifty times $2,500 and they would pay us that much in premium and that much less in taxes. But the same result would not at all follow in the case of a company alongside of them. I could not defend it, and so I am asking my colleague to move that the deleted words be restored.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
Well, I
am just not convinced. The situation in England is not exactly the same as it is in Canada. There is one vital difference in England, that there is no corporation tax 
there; they take 100 per cent above the standard profits, but they leave to the companies the standard profits. If you apply that system to the people of Canada, I think they would be agreeable to it. It would leave in their own hands, not in the hands of the government to be passed back at some future date, the capital necessary to rehabilitate their premises, their machinery, their plant and so forth and to provide the employment which will be so necessary in this country after the war.
The minister says it will be a payment out of capital. Yes, it will be a payment out of their capital, but an impairment of their capital. What is the depreciation he does allow? Depreciation is set up for the protection of the capital invested, so that it can be written down and protected. That is the underlying reason for allowing the write-off, because if there were no depreciation of the capital assets there would not be any justification for writing off one cent.
The minister has now stated in explicit terms that he is bound to have this put through. I hesitate to hold up the committee on a discussion of this question. I want to say that the thing is not so wholly one-sided as the minister is endeavouring to convince the membership to-night. I am rather shocked to think that he takes so extreme an attitude as he does; and I come back to this, that the only reason the minister is doing this is that he needs the money and is going to get it, and he does not care whom it hurts. If that is not conscription of wealth, I should like to know what is.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: It is fairer than the other.

Well, of course it is perfectly true that the government will be paying 100 per cent of the premiums in connection with companies that are in the excess profits tax bracket, but after you have squeezed 100 per cent of the blood from a stone you cannot squeeze any more. If you have a new cost in connection with your business, which is necessary to preserve your property, and for which you must pay premiums, obviously if there is nothing left, if all the money is taken away, the money for the additional cost must come from some other source, which means that it must come from taxation. That is why we are in this very peculiar situation, and I think the minister is looking at it in a rather wrong light. It is by reason of the war that we have this peculiar position of a company incurring additional expense, while the only source from which that expense can be met is from what otherwise would go for taxation. That is an effect of the war, and of the excess profits tax. So is this need for war risk insurance an effect of the war. Surely, therefore, the war should be allowed to bear some proportion of the cost resulting from the risk which is brought about by the war; yet the minister says that because some companies will be allowed to offset only 40 per cent of the premium against their taxation, while others, if they were allowed to put it in their expense accounts, would be allowed to offset 100 per cent, some inequality or injustice is thereby created. No one is more willing than I that it should be undermined as far as necessary in order to provide money for the war; but if we are going to look to private enterprise to carry the burden after the war, and not have state socialism, then we must keep the corporate structure in a reasonable degree of health. So the situation still is that a corporation or a business must provide out of its annual earnings sufficient to keep itself intact. It must allow for the wearing out of its equipment, of the machine which produces some material; it must provide for ordinary fire insurance, wages, materials and everything else. In the same way we have an unusual expense occasioned by the war, and a corporation should be allowed to provide for that_ expense as a charge against its annual earnings. Now we come to the very peculiar situation to which I referred in the beginning, and which the minister makes so much of in his appeal for fairness to all companies. subtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES-ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext:
First of all I want to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) upon introducing this most comprehensive piece of legislation. I should like to call the attention of the committee to the fact that education is a matter of supreme importance to the nation, but it is a subject which has occupied very little time in this house, either during this session or at other sessions. Because of that fact I crave the indulgence of the minister and the committee while I set forth a few facts pertaining to the bill.
The bill provides for financial support for education in the vocational field, and I would solicit the support of every hon. member for the bill. In case anyone is a little dubious because of the fact that education is a provincial matter, I would point out that this is not an innovation. We had the Agricultural Instruction Act of 1913 which provided for $10,000,000 from the federal treasury to aid agricultural education. We had the Technical Education Act of 1919 which provided for $10,000,000. Then we had the Vocational Education Act of 1931 which provided for $750,000, but which was never put into effect. We have had the youth training programme, the war emergency programme and other means by which the federal government in the past has supported education within the provinces. This bill simply extends the financial service of the federal government to education within the provincial field in line with the immediate and future needs of this nation. The object of the bill will be evident to every hon. member as it is discussed or comes up for review section by section. I shall not take the time to review the various objects of the bill, but I would point out that it does not provide for any interference on the part of the federal government with the right of the provinces in the matter of education. The bill provides at every step for cooperation and agreement between the federal government and the provincial departments of education.
However, the bill does recognize in a more general way than has heretofore been the situation the responsibility of the federal government toward education and the national importance of education. In my judgment that is a matter which should receive more consideration in this house than it has in the past.
I think every member of this house will agree with me when I say that equal educational opportunity is the democratic birthright of every Canadian child, and by "equal" I do not in any sense mean "uniform." I believe that the educational opportunities afforded the young Canadian boy or girl in any province of

this country should be limited only by the ability^ of that boy or girl to profit by the educational opportunities and by the ability of the province and the nation to provide those educational opportunities.
Education is a national responsibility because of its importance as a factor in Canadian unity. Within the past few weeks we have heard a great deal in this house about the lack of unity in this country, and we have had occasion to deplore that in spite of the fact that the two races have been living together for three hundred years, this country has not yet become a unified nation. On a former occasion I deplored the fact that the lack of unity within this country could be charged to a large extent to our systems of education. We must educate our boys and girls as citizens of Canada and not as citizens of the maritimes or of Quebec or of Ontario or of our western provinces. Nor must we educate them as citizens of any particular city or province.
We should draw from the races that make up the population of this country, not only from the French and English but from the other races, the best that they have in culture and in democratic principles. Democracy is not a monopoly of the English-speaking races. There is much that we can learn as democratic citizens from the French and other races represented in this country.
Education has become a national responsibility because of the movement to-day of population from province to province, from the rural districts to the urban districts.
It has been estimated that one out of every three persons in Canada to-day is living in a province other than that in which he was born. It therefore becomes a matter of extreme importance to each province within the dominion that every boy and every girl in every other province should receive a minimum standard of education. Every child in every province is a potential citizen, a potential asset or a potential liability to every other province. Education is a national responsibility because of the complexity of modern life, and because of that complexity it becomes important that every child in every province should receive a reasonable minimum standard of education.
Canada to-day is called upon to compete in the markets of the world. We are called upon to compete in the councils of the world. The boys and girls who were born in one province are called upon to compete in the labour markets of this country with boys and girls born and brought up in other

provinces. All this would indicate that the education of any child in any province is of importance to every other province.
Canadian boys and girls, regardless of race, should be given the best possible education which the country can afford to give them and which they are capable of profiting by.
I should like to call the attention of the committee for a few moments to a few of the shortcomings of our present educational system, particularly in the matter of administration and finance. The administration and financing of education as it exists in Canada to-day is not very far different from the system which was set up in the pioneer days of this country, in the days when the one and only mode of transportation was the ox-cart. To-day we are attempting to administer a stream-lined system of education by the old administrative and financial methods adopted in the ox-cart days. We still leave our schools to be administered by a board elected from a very small school area, the same type of school area which was set up in the pioneer days of this country. That system still prevails to a large extent all across this dominion, with the single exception of the one province of Alberta and parts of British Columbia. We still leave those small municipalities and those small school sections to bear as much as 80 and 90 per cent of the cost of education within the schools of that area. As a result, we find that in the cities and in the prosperous rural communities we get good modern schools, with teachers reasonably well paid. But when we get into the poorer communities adjoining the wealthier ones and into the poorer rural areas, we find a deplorable situation.

I am going to say only a word or two; I am not going to make a speech. I spoke about vocational training away back in 1940, and I was pleased to see that this bill was coming up. I was on the committee which considered this bill, and I feel that it was thoroughly gone through in committee. We had many meetings; we sat for weeks on this bill.
One thing about vocational training which struck me when I went through different schools was that it was not confined to young boys; in some instances grey-haired and baldheaded men were taking this training. They were anxious to learn in order to get jobs, and they were obtaining jobs in various plants.
Vocational Training

They were willing to take the classes even if they had to attend at two, three, four or five o'clock in the morning. I believe that the Minister of Labour will tell the committee later that in some places there was a series of classes sitting the whole twenty-four hours. In one school an Italian fruit-dealer, anxious to do something for Canada, his adopted home, [DOT] but unable to get into the army, was taking vocational training with a view to doing his bit in a munition plant. Inside seven or eight weeks he was able to take a position in the plant. He underwent an additional course, and to-day he is a machinist, doing a wonderful job on 3'7-inch guns.
In these schools vocational training is given to girls and young women, including married women. It is not a case of training them so much as to get them accustomed to working in a shop, so that when they go into a plant they will not be nervous. These women have turned out to be wonderful workers, in many instances better than the men. I was surprised to see in one plant girls working on vertical turret lathes, something which the plant manager never thought girls could do. and doing a wonderful job. I saw one girl at a vertical turret lathe teaching two men how to run it. The girls are coming along all the time. A great number of them are married, and many have come from the farms. That may be why the farmers to-day need all the help we can give them. Indeed, not only the women but many of the farmers have left the land because it was not providing them with a living.
